source.title: Fisher Width: A Geometric Measure of Complexity on Statistical Manifolds

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether Fisher width tracks a measured generalization gap, using a different complexity measure from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: Section 7.4 reports generalization-gap results and their relation to Fisher width. Other findings about estimator accuracy and Fisher geometry do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study measures Fisher width and generalization-gap scaling in regression models. None of its results tests V1–V8. Fisher width is neither network width (V2) nor magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness (V7); related sharpness research is discussed but not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase accurately summarizes Section 7.4: measured gaps approximately follow 1/√n and fall below a Fisher-width envelope whose constant is fitted empirically. The paper's broader conclusion introduces Fisher width as a local geometric complexity measure, establishes conditional generalization bounds, and validates estimators in regression models; extension to neural networks remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Studies Fisher-width complexity and generalization-gap scaling in MNIST softmax regression; it does not test the listed interventions or magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported gap-versus-1/√n fit varies by regularization level; Fisher width growth across training sizes is smaller at λ = 1 than at λ = 10⁻³.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST softmax-regression gaps are approximately linear in 1/√n, with R² values 0.935–0.987. All 28 averaged points fall below an empirically calibrated Fisher-width/√n envelope.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested softmax-regression setting, generalization gaps exhibit approximate inverse-square-root sample-size scaling and fit a calibrated Fisher-width envelope.

fits_no_version.finding: Fisher width increases between n = 200 and 20,000 by factors of 5.97 at λ = 0.001 and 1.19 at λ = 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger L2 regularization reduces the growth of estimated Fisher width with training-set size in MNIST softmax regression.

record.problems: The reported generalization-gap scaling experiment is limited to one model class and MNIST; the envelope constant is calibrated empirically. The full softmax parameterization is non-identifiable, with the analysis interpreted through a quotient-space formulation.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from Section 7.4. Other experiment results concern Fisher-width estimator accuracy or stability rather than a listed claim version or the measured generalization gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Network-width sweeps beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and the effects of tuning or optimizer changes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance in convolutional networks at comparable training loss, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All seven numerical results match the supplied text. Their states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because none measures a listed effect. No additional results bearing on those versions were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout comparisons and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations and comparisons with sharpness or norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
